title: Integrating mitogenomes, morphology, and ecology reveals depth-structured diversification and two new species of deep-sea Bargmannia siphonophores (Cnidaria: Hydrozoa)
content:
Abstract
Open-ocean biodiversity is structured by subtle environmental gradients rather than obvious geographic barriers, yet how genomes, morphology, and ecology interact during diversification in such systems remains unclear. Here we use Bargmannia siphonophores (Cnidaria: Hydrozoa) as a tractable model system for understanding the evolution of deep-sea pelagic biodiversity. Using museum specimens, genome-skimming data, and in situ observations and collections from remotely operated vehicles, we resolve species boundaries, clarify historical taxonomy, and describe two new species, B. marlena sp. nov. and B. pyrosa sp. nov. Our phylogenomic analyses recovered two major lineages within Bargmannia, one of which exhibits pronounced acceleration of mitochondrial genome evolution. This genomic divergence coincided with a transition to monoecy, suggesting a potential link between mitochondrial evolution and sexual system shift. Using geometric morphometrics we show that nectophore shape variation is strongly structured by phylogeny and follows lineage-specific allometric trajectories, while comparative cnidome analyses indicate functional divergence associated with differences in nematocyst size and tentillum architecture. Finally, although Bargmannia species overlap geographically, their distributions are structured along depth gradients, supporting vertical niche partitioning as an important driver of speciation in the open ocean. Together, these findings show how deep-sea biodiversity emerges from the interplay of genomic innovation, morphological divergence, and depth structuring.
